rows.source: DVSA trailer and caravan towing safety
rows.verified: Drivers should complete basic safety checks every time they tow a trailer, caravan or horsebox.

rows.source: DVSA trailer and caravan towing safety
rows.verified: The trailer coupling must be correctly attached at the appropriate height in accordance with manufacturer instructions.

rows.source: DVSA trailer and caravan towing safety
rows.verified: A breakaway cable or secondary coupling must be serviceable, correctly connected and clear of the road surface.

rows.source: DVSA trailer and caravan towing safety
rows.verified: Trailer wheels and tyres must be legal, correctly inflated and free from unsafe damage or deterioration.

rows.source: DVSA trailer and caravan towing safety
rows.verified: Lights, indicators, electrical connections and the registration plate must remain visible and operational.
A vehicle and trailer must not be overloaded, and the load must be distributed and secured safely within manufacturer limits.

rows.source: DVSA trailer and caravan towing safety
rows.verified: A vehicle towing on a motorway with three or more lanes must not use the right-hand lane.
If a trailer begins to snake, the driver should ease off the accelerator and reduce speed gently rather than braking harshly.

rows.source: DVSA trailer and caravan towing safety
rows.verified: Towing risk depends on vehicle and trailer compatibility, load distribution, coupling, tyres, brakes, speed, wind, road and driver competence.
Towing evidence is combination-, load-, route-, weather-, maintenance- and driver-specific and is not an exact parcel-level collision probability.
Goods carried in an HGV, trailer, van or car must be loaded, transported and unloaded safely.
Vehicle operators, drivers and consignors all have responsibilities in deciding and applying a safe transport method.
Loads should be placed against the headboard or within 30 centimetres of it wherever practicable, or restrained against forward movement by suitable alternatives.
Standard curtains on a curtainsider are primarily weather protection and are not designed as the main load-securing system.
An XL-rated body only provides its intended restraint when documented construction and positive-fit loading conditions are met.
Abnormal loads should have a movement-specific plan and a combination of suitable lashings and physical restraints.
Unstable or top-heavy loads must be supported or placed in a suitable frame because lashings alone cannot make an unstable load safe.
Loading equipment carried on the vehicle, including pump trucks, is itself part of the load and must be secured during travel.
Load movement risk depends on mass, centre of gravity, friction, vehicle body, restraint rating, gaps, route, braking and unloading method.
Load-securing evidence is vehicle-, load-, restraint-, route-, handling- and condition-specific and is not an exact parcel-level road-casualty probability.
